title: Attention as prayer
hook: Simone Weil held that attention, taken to its highest, is prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, the serenity prayer: serenity, courage, and the wisdom between them. Your line was know the difference.

A student sits over a geometry problem and can't crack it. The hour runs out. The page is a mess of crossed-out lines. Was the hour wasted? Simone Weil, a French philosopher deeply drawn to Christ, said no. In an essay written for students, she argued that real effort of attention is never lost, even when the problem stays unsolved. What's being trained, she said, isn't geometry. It's attention. And attention, taken to its highest, is the same thing as prayer.

Weil means something specific by attention. Not frowning. Not clenching your jaw. She describes it as more like waiting: holding your own thoughts back, empty and ready, so that what's really there can come in. Straining gets in the way. That's why she cared about schoolwork. A Latin translation, a math proof: done with real attention, she thought, each one stretches the same capacity the soul uses to turn toward God. Then she turns it toward people. Love of neighbor, Weil wrote, comes down to being able to ask someone, what are you going through? And then actually to look and listen, without rushing to fix them. She thought that kind of attention was rare, and close to a miracle. Luke has a scene she'd recognize, one this path met earlier. Jesus is a guest in a home. Martha is busy serving. Her sister Mary "sat at Jesus' feet, and heard his word." Martha complains, and Jesus answers: "Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part." Readers take this in different ways. Some stress that Martha's work is good too, just anxious. Some hear Mary as a picture of prayer itself. Weil's lens adds one thing: Mary isn't doing nothing. She's attending. A phone buzzing face-down on the table. A friend talking while you plan your reply. A prayer said while thinking about lunch. Weil's point lands on all of them: the opposite of prayer may not be doubt. It may be distraction.

Choose one sound in the room, a clock, traffic, the hum of a fridge, your own breathing, and listen to it only, without naming or explaining it. When your mind slides off, notice where it went and come back without scolding; attention, for Weil, is a kind of waiting. If you pray, you can let this listening be your prayer, with no words at all.
Attention as prayer. Simone Weil's claim that attention, taken to its highest, is the same as prayer: open, waiting, and fully there, for God and for a neighbor.
Your line: attention is prayer. Even an hour on an unsolved problem trains it. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Christians practice prayer as attention, sitting quietly before God without words, or praying while giving full attention to a task or a person; Simone Weil's essays are read in many settings as a guide to this.

notes: All of Weil is paraphrased (her English translations are not public domain): attention 'taken to its highest' is prayer; unsolved problems still train attention; attention as waiting, not muscular effort; love of neighbor as asking 'what are you going through?'; such attention is rare, close to a miracle. Please check each paraphrase against the school-studies essay.
'A French philosopher deeply drawn to Christ' is chosen because Weil never asked for baptism; confirm the wording is fair.

Original: French 'attente' (waiting) with the title Attente de Dieu; a French word, not a biblical one. Confirm the title and that the note doesn't overstate a link between 'attention' and 'attente' (no etymology is claimed).
